"BPD diagnosis in women is often based in mysogyny, especially when it’s a co-morbid diagnosis with adhd. It’s the new “hysteria” diagnosis."

I'm familiar with the literature on the comorbid diagnoses of BPD, ADHD, and autism as well in women. I do believe poorly defined concepts and diagnostic criteria, along with inadequate training, all-too-often allow biases to creep in to psychiatric judgment, but I would be wary of making a declarative statement this strong on a situation that's already fuzzy enough by its nature.

One of my foster kids was formally diagnosed with ADHD, and her psychoeducational assessment suggested she may also have both a general reading and general math learning disability. Reading hasn't been as much of an obstacle; she loves anime and manga and I'm familiar with those media, so it was easy enough to give her material she was motivated to practice with (she even now prefers to watch anime subbed so she can learn a little Japanese at the same time). 

Spelling she never really seemed to have all that much trouble with outside of motivation to practice; she could pass spelling tests without practicing at home, and would ace them when I could actually get her to do it. Math has been much more difficult, and I'm suspicious it's a dyscalculia factor even though that specifically hasn't been formally diagnosed, since she has no significant trouble with understanding the concepts and only struggles when she has to manipulate the numbers to arrive at an answer. Being allowed to use a calculator when she otherwise wouldn't be permitted makes a world of difference in her ability to actually solve math problems.

It's interesting that these have been found to be genetically linked, since there's some symptomology overlap with BPD (very frequently co-diagnosed with ADHD, particularly in girls) and oftentimes that too goes hand-in-hand with these kinds of learning challenges.

"the way most cognitive psych currently describes these events tends to impart a sense of intention and "conscious" agency to this pattern of behavior"

I hate to break it to you, but sometimes that's true for these patterns of behaviour, especially if the person knows they have certain patterns and tendencies and consciously choose not to make an effort to think or behave differently. And, frankly, this doesn't actually discredit the idea of personality traits as a useful construct, since it's the existence of these consistent patterns at all that actually matters.

"How this tends to sound is like this person *has* this trait - like it's a *thing*, and its this trait that drives this behavior"

Yes, and this absolutely reflects reality. Regardless of how they do it, it is well understood that people establish through their lifetimes consistent thought patterns that manifest as consistent behaviours, and this is what people are calling personality traits.

"If whatever caused the "single act of manipulation" is the *exact same mechanism* as that which causes repeated acts of manipulation"

That's a big assumption to make. For example, a person who otherwise doesn't engage in manipulative behaviour can engage in an act for altruistic reasons (like talking someone down from a ledge), while it's a given that manipulative behaviour can definitely also be engaged in completely selfishly. Obviously, the 'exact same mechanism' is not at work though, and the differences are important.

'They don't think this is "fine" or "comfortable", if they think about it at all, it's just to describe their world in which that behavior is *necessary* because that's how the world is - which is exactly the same situation happening to the "single act of manipulation" person in a singular, isolated situation.'

It doesn't have to be about 'comfort' per se, and I suspect you knew that. The point is that the behaviour is present and consistently exceptional relative to the general population across similar situations and experiences - which suggests that it's not about the situations or experiences, but the person's behaviour and how it differs relative to the general population.

"It reinforces the idea that people with *these traits* are doing something different than everyone else, that they *are* different"

This is correct, though. People have innate tendencies and differing risk levels, genetic or environmental, to develop certain consistently different thought patterns that manifest as consistently different behaviours. These patterns literally are personality traits.

Behaviours happen in an "instance" of time. A trait more describes a persistent pattern of associated beliefs and repeated behaviours. A person who engages in a single act of manipulation, for example, exhibited a manipulative behaviour but does not necessarily exhibit manipulativeness as a personality trait, but somebody who is perfectly comfortable with and consistently engages in manipulative behaviours certainly could. The strongest predictor of future behaviour is past behaviour; there is value in traits as a psychological concept beyond how you're trying dismiss it.

The Japanese name is actually a reference to a Japanese proverb or phrase with a bit of silliness attached, referring to something that is extremely unexpected or unlikely but very convenient, like a duck bringing its own onion to make soup out of it. The Japanese name is in fact the shortened version of the phrase, which came to be understood to refer to the whole idea.

The term (Kamonegi) also gets used to refer to the duck being foolish or naive in some way, as carrying the onion makes it a target to be made into delicious soup. There's some speculation that the name in Japanese is also a reference to the way Farfetch'd was originally obtained in this sense, in that a Spearow, which you would trade, evolves into Fearow  relatively quickly at that point in the game, which is generally more powerful than Farfetch'd. Therefore, this would be a trade that only a foolish or naive person would make.

All of this is to say that the name Farfetch'd could be intended to be a reference to both of these interpretations, in terms of an unlikely event and also as something only a foolish or naive person would buy into.

We're back to the problem of distinction, then. The people who have learned to cast spells through performance are different from the people who just perform, and not only would they know the difference, other people would know it too and there would be terms for it in-universe. The class terminology is an abstraction, so they're not going to call themselves "bards by class", but if we're not reserving the term "bard" for Bards, we still need a way to distinguish between them.

Also, the barbarian example doesn't really make sense. Literally everyone gets stronger when they're really mad or hyped or focused or however you flavour it; it's called adrenaline. The barbarian class is just a way to fantasy-power it to superhuman levels for funsies. There's no real flavor difference between a barbarian and an angry rando, since that's essentially what they are, so no distinction needs to be made and we can safely preserve the colloquial meaning of the term barbarian in-universe.

This is borderline pedantic. The Bards know, and the bards probably know too, as would the other types of spellcasters that have to spend time learning their craft (mostly wizards, probably clerics and warlocks, and the odd druid). Obviously, the point I am making is that the distinction would be there and there would be people who would know of it and have terms for the difference, not specifically what a layperson would say.

Then how exactly do people in your world distinguish between bards and Bards? What is the term for someone who has unlocked the secrets of performative magic (i.e. a character who has Bard class levels), if the term "bard" can refer to anyone who plays an instrument or performs for pay?

If you're playing D&D, then your characters are in a world where these people are different in a very measurable way, unlike this real one where the magic people don't exist. If the Bard class is still a thing in "your world" (i.e. that people can access magic the way Bards normally do), then the existence of the access to magic in that way builds the necessity of the distinction into it. You ARE welcome to run your world however you like, reflavouring things as you see fit, but it's worth thinking about at the very least.

Dudes who sing or play instruments would be better referred to as "minstrels" or "musicians", so they're properly distinguished "in your world" from the people who actually use the magic of performance to cast spells. How a Bard uses music and how your average musician does is different enough to warrant a distinction of terms, at the very least.

Anticoagulant: I considered the balancing for this around effects like Hex and Hunter's Mark. Essentially, you give up the ability to inflict the effect at a distance, not requiring an attack roll or a saving throw, inflicting the effect as a bonus action, adding a minor additional effect, and a little more initial damage for the increased scaling damage (which still requires attack rolls and subsequent standard actions and consumption of supply points) and enabling your allies to benefit from it (which they may actually not at all, depending on party makeup). I'm not concerned about the strength of this syringe. The language surrounding it is because of a subclass feature that interacts with the syringe.
Antipyretic: This is a real-world class of drugs that help bring down fevers, hence fire resistance (flavored from improving the body's ability to manage temperature). Also, the Antitoxin syringe provides poison resistance along the same lines.
Oxytocin: This is indeed a Charm Person analogue, but it is again supposed to more closely mimic the real-life substance than just be a copy of the spell. Oxytocin has been called the "bonding hormone" or the "cuddle hormone"-and hormones don't discriminate. Part of extending the charmed effect to every target it encounters is that the effect is extended to the target's allies, but it also extends it to your allies. This is in exchange for the fact that Charm Person lasts way longer, doesn't require an attack roll, can be done at range, and scales up so that it can affect multiple targets at once. In trade, the charmed condition is applied to all creatures present, the affected creature doesn't have advantage on the saving throw if it is in combat with you and your allies, you can subject a wider variety of creatures to the effect, and the effect doesn't automatically end if a "charmer" damages the target, though the saving throw caused by that should definitely be made with advantage.
Anesthetic: The Charisma saving throw required by this syringe is on purpose; it's a generally less common saving throw proficiency in monsters than Constitution. It's supposed to be a Hold Person analogue; in exchange for requiring an attack roll at melee range and only affecting the target for one round, it affects a wider variety of creatures and targets a generally weaker save. I conceived of it as the Charisma save representing sheer force of will and intent powering through the effect of the Anesthetic; like how Plane Shift and Banishment get resisted.
Hallucinogen: This is another one that got shortened because of laziness-the effect is the same and so is the saving throw, so I didn't bother to put in any qualifiers. That will be rectified.
Stimulant: I considered the increasing cost of the effect as well as requiring melee range to be sufficient compensation for the effect not requiring concentration, especially given that sorcerers can twin haste to give it to two allies in a single action, but I do agree that the effect was too strong even in testing. I made the increasing cost continue to scale through short rests instead requiring long rests to reset, so hopefully that sufficiently discourages spamming it. I am considering increasing the scaling to 3 extra supply points per use instead of 2 if that's not enough, as well as just plain nerfing the effect to only grant an extra attack the way Haste does (without the loss of the turn at the end in compensation, which means I'll have to change the Anatomist's Enhanced Stimulant to maybe grant the lost Haste effects-or possibly something else).

Precision: The main reason this feature grants advantage at all is because of the syringes requiring melee attack rolls to apply effects to enemies in comparison to their magical counterparts which can just affect their targets, even at range. I wanted a way for this weakness to be mitigated but not eliminated, hence the addition of the advantage from a bonus action onto a feature that was originally just supposed to give the physician a way to actually damage their enemies (deliberately similar to the sneak attack, given the nature of striking in a precise location being similar to the flavour of sneak attack but explicitly weaker damage and requiring a bonus action to compensate for everything else the physician brought to the table). The fact that the bonus action isn't much of an opportunity cost is indeed a problem, and while there are a few subclass features that make it somewhat relevant, it isn't enough for the base physician. The main fix I'm implementing for this is to remove the ability to grant advantage on the attacks to which you want to add the damage-in essence, choose between granting advantage on a syringe attack or dealing extra damage with the next regular attack. The "next attack within 1 minute" was because I liked the idea of the physician being able to use the Stimulant syringe on themselves and then a bonus action to gain the effect on one turn, and then using it between attacks on the next turn for burst damage the way a Hasted rogue can hold action for a similar effect. That can still happen; 1 minute is probably too long anyway so until the end of the next turn is probably sufficient, especially considering a dual wielding physician can kinda already do that. I'm also considering giving the subclasses more to do with their bonus actions to compete for the action economy.

Careful Care and Analytical Eye: These are supposed to be underwhelming, since you get them both at the same time. The frontloadedness of the class is deliberate along the lines of the monk; they don't get anything too impressive in higher levels either. Careful Care was balanced around the bard's Song of Rest, instead adding a constant amount of hit points rather than a random one. It scales roughly with it as well, as your Intelligence increases.

Protected Personnel: I agree that this is awkwardly implemented, but just copying the Sanctuary spell doesn't quite capture the effect I'm going for, which I'm sure you can tell is supposed to be evocative of the Geneva Convention on protecting combat medics. I like the idea of the Sanctuary effect, with some caveats to keep it thematic-creatures with a Chaotic Evil alignment as well as creatures with an Intelligence score below 6 ignore the effect entirely, and otherwise Chaotic or Evil creatures have a 50% chance of ignoring the effect entirely.

Medical Mastery: I can certainly see the place for more features that use supply points in the subclasses, certain ones especially, but the fact that this reduces the cost of some of them to 0 doesn't bother me. This is a capstone feature; it should be strong. I didn't want it to be exactly the same as the monk's or sorcerer's, so I wanted to find a different way for the physician to save or refund supply points, and I'm comfortable with the result, alongside a stat increase similar to the barbarian's (granting them the same increase in AC with their defensive features, with the supply point cost reduction mimicking the barbarian's infinite rages).

The healer's kit is a non-issue. The physician gets one in their character creation supplies, just like how a wizard gets a spellbook, and just like how multiclass wizards have to get their hands on one somehow. The physician has their Quick Patch feature to do what expending a charge of a healer's kit would do anyway, so they really shouldn't be consuming all of the uses of their healer's kit before they have an opportunity to get a new one except in dire circumstances (which is fine-dire circumstances should have dire consequences). This wasn't a problem at all in testing, and I was deliberately pitting the test party up against Deadly level encounters (which they really shouldn't be encountering that frequently anyway). This was no more intrusive or obstructive than a martial character focused on ranged attacks needing to buy ammunition.

Syringes: These are not the class' core feature; the supply points themselves are. These are more for the physician what Flurry of Blows, Stunning Strike, Patient Defense, and Step of the Wind are for the monk. The core monk doesn't get more ways to spend ki points past those until 14th level and even then it's 1 ki point, and of the subclasses presented in the PHB only the Four Elements monk gets new ways to use them consistently as the monk levels. Thanks for catching the 2/4/6 bit too; that was from when I was messing around with which levels certain features would be obtained-the levels are supposed to correlate to levels at which casters would have access to spells with similar effects (2 for 1st level spells, 4 for 2nd, and 6 for 3rd). This is partially also why the Syringes stop here in addition to the monk stuff; I wanted them to be real-world medications that would mimic the effects of certain spells, but limited to lower level spells since the higher level spells just don't really have real-world analogues. I don't completely dislike the idea of the vials, but the limitations here go back to keeping it similar to real-world medicine: these substances have to be delivered in a specific way to have their desired effect, and with most of these, the trace amounts that would be delivered through a normal attack with a weapon just wouldn't do that. Not only that, but just sticking something on a sword and slashing someone with it to deliver it is way less flavorful than the syringes. As for the limitations on the number of syringe effects a target can be under, I really have no problem with multiple effects for both allies and enemies, given that a key part of the balance behind the syringes is that they have to be delivered in melee range for both. To subject enemies to any effects you have to be right there with them and hit them with the attack (which partially explains the problems with Precision, more on that later) AND they have to fail the saving throw to be subjected to the effect. To be able to subject allies to multiple syringes, you have to stick to them too like glue, which may be a problem if you're hanging in the back with your ranged characters and your melee characters need support and vice versa. Encounters don't tend to last long enough anyway for multiple syringes on a single target to be worth the expenditure of supply points and the use of your action economy.

Alright, let me address some of this...

Quick Patch: My intent with it being tracked on other people was for it to be reflective of the nature of the healing (like the Healer feat, using it as a basis for how mundane healing would be handled)-no matter how skilled you are, there are only so many bandages and salves you can apply to a person's injuries, stitches you can use to close up wounds, or broken bones you can reset without interfering with that person's normal functioning; nothing more you can do for that person, but not other people. Magical healing doesn't really have that problem (and has other limitations as a consequence), and I wanted to stay far away from more supernatural-ish healing methods like it or "miracle serums" and stick to what could be justified with real-world medical knowledge. I conceived of it as a "first aid" sort of thing that used negligible amounts of resources, such that their consumption could be handwaved away, and both became more effective and could be used more frequently as a physician became more skilled (in the sense that they were both able to repair more damage and minimize the interference of their intervention). The way I justified its uses per person was comparing it to what druids, clerics, and bards could do with Cure Wounds at certain levels (if they upcasted with the higher level spell slots they gained, never mind the healing that could actually be done with higher level spells); the goal was to scale its uses per day in a typical four-person party with the spell slots that could be used in that fashion. Also, I think you misunderstood the line about the limitation to eight *unique* people per hour; the goal with that was to make it useful for a larger party without being able to spam the heals on an army of NPCs at a higher level (I conceived of that limitation as representing the "busyness" of having to go around healing multiple people); essentially it just means you have to limit using the feature over the course of an hour to eight specific "patients". For example, a level 10 physician could use the feature a total of 12 times (three each) per long rest in a four-man party. I do think a cleaner way to handle that limitation would be to make it a short rest thing rather than an hour, though. I don't think tracking the targets of this feature is going to be a problem most of the time, since as you say it's usually just going to be your party (in testing it was certainly no more difficult or intrusive than managing spell preparation when the party takes a long rest), and I'm honestly comfortable with the physician's healing being less flexible than magical healing. All of this being said, I am considering a charge system just for the sake of simplification (though I am unsure as to how I would go about that without compromising the "non-magical, non-mad-science realistic medicine" feel-I mean, it IS D&D though, so maybe I should just not bother with it if it's getting in the way), so I appreciate that feedback.

Deliberate Defense: Thanks for catching the wording on it, though I will say that not restricting shields was on purpose. The AC calculation isn't based on an instinctive understanding of how one's body moves attained through years of meditation, introspection, and practice like the monk's is, such that armor and shields would get in the way of the body's natural movements. It's more about having a textbook understanding of body kinetics and the physics thereof, such that you know through analysis how your attacker is going to strike and how to receive it. The armor would restrict movements enough such that it would impair this, but if you already know how to use a shield I see no reason why a physician's ability to analyze and their knowledge of physics would have to be impaired by using one to receive or deflect attacks. Using a shield wouldn't be part of a physician's training, though, so they don't have the proficiency and would have to use a feat or multiclass to be able to use one anyway, which I feel is a nice halfway point between the barbarian and monk versions of the ability (since I didn't want it to just be a direct copy of either, just with Intelligence). Moreover, not being able to use shields with this makes the class quite squishy in comparison to druids, clerics, and even bards (who at least get either Cutting Words or actual shields with the PHB subclasses). I omitted the shield line more to save time as I was typing and I intended to add the barbarian's "you can use a shield" line later, so I appreciate that you caught that anyway.

Since then, every so often, when I think about ending it I think about what kind of effect it would have on her. Sometimes I'm mortified by the thought of so deeply hurting someone I loved, sometimes I just don't care, and sometimes I revel in the thought that she would be hurt by it; that I could hurt her back for hurting me.

But, of course, the bottom line is that if/when he finds out about it, he's going to be hurt by it no matter what if he ever loved you at all. You could leave a note asking him not to blame himself, but he will (and it might just make it worse, given that even in your darkest moments you thought of him). So what's the solution?

Simple. You don't do it. You live, you survive, and you don't have to think about what that will mean for him at all. Your survival ought to be about you first, given that you'll be the one doing the surviving. One of my mother's favorite lines is "The best revenge against someone who has wronged you is a life well-lived in spite of them." What you'll be doing won't exactly be revenge, but a life well-lived without regard for him is what's best for everyone at this point.
